subChunks.title: Capstone — Professional Research Dissertation

storyBeats.txt: This is the end of the pathway, Theodora said. Not the end of learning — there is no such thing. But the end of the structured curriculum. From here, your development is self-directed.

The capstone asks you to demonstrate everything: research at professional standard, written to professional standard, with professional citations, professional ethics, and professional judgment about your own limitations.

You are not just documenting an ancestor. You are modelling what genealogical scholarship looks like at its best. Clear. Honest. Documented. Reasoned. Complete — and honest about what remains incomplete.

The thousand names I carry are not titles. They are the names of all the people I have helped to find — all the threads I have traced back to their origins. Yours is among them now. Go and add to the record.

subChunks.hookHtml:
You have completed the Genealogy Lead pathway — covering professional standards, client work, proof argument writing, citation practice, peer review, teaching, society leadership, archival preservation, business practice, legal obligations, ethics, publishing, presentation, mentoring, emerging technologies, and international collaboration. This capstone draws on everything.

The Lead-level capstone is a professional research dissertation: a substantial, fully documented genealogical investigation of a specific research question, written to the standard of a journal submission or BCG portfolio piece. It demonstrates not just research competency but the full range of professional skills — from initial problem definition through to a final GPS-compliant written argument, with explicit attention to ethics, limitations, and the contribution to knowledge the work makes.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Professional Research Dissertation

The Lead capstone is not a proof argument (though it contains one). It is a professional research dissertation — a self-contained document that demonstrates the full range of professional genealogical competency at the Lead level. It has six components:

  1. Research context and question: An introduction explaining the genealogical and historical context of the research question, why it matters, and what existing research (if any) exists on this question. This section situates the work in the broader field.
  2. Methodology: A comprehensive account of the research strategy — what sources were selected and why, what alternatives were considered, what the logical sequence of investigation was. This is not a chronological research log but a reasoned strategic account.
  3. Evidence analysis: Application of the GPS evidence analysis framework — source, information, and evidence classification — to every significant piece of evidence. Conflicts identified and addressed. DNA evidence (if used) integrated with documentary evidence.
  4. Proof argument: A formal GPS-compliant proof argument addressing the specific research question, meeting all five GPS elements.
  5. Ethical reflection: Discussion of any ethical considerations raised by the research — living people, sensitive discoveries, community protocols, data protection. What ethical decisions were made and why.
  6. Professional contribution and future directions: What does this research contribute to the field? What remains unresolved? What further investigation is warranted? How might this work be published or presented?

Length and Standard

The dissertation should be 1,200–1,800 words (excluding citations and appendices). Every factual claim must be cited to an Evidence Explained standard. The proof argument section must demonstrate GPS compliance. The ethical reflection section must address at least one genuine ethical consideration raised by the research.

Assessment is against four criteria (25% each): research methodology; evidence analysis; proof argument quality; and professional reflection (ethics + contribution).

Scenarios

Choose ONE of the following scenarios:

Scenario A: The Immigrant's Identity

Rosa Ferreira (b. c.1895 in Portugal, d. 1968 in Massachusetts, USA) appears in the 1920 and 1930 US censuses as Rosa Ferreira, born Portugal, married to Manuel Ferreira. Her death certificate gives her birthplace as 'Azores, Portugal' and her parents as 'unknown'. Her granddaughter has tested on AncestryDNA; her highest match is a second cousin (195 cM) with a tree showing the Melo and Bettencourt families in São Miguel, Azores.

Research task: Establish Rosa's identity — full name, precise origin in the Azores, and parents — using DNA and documentary evidence. Your dissertation should include: the research question; methodology (what sources would you use in what order and why); analysis of the DNA evidence using the Leeds Method; what Portuguese/Azorean records are available and how you would access them; a proof argument for Rosa's identity based on your research; and ethical reflection on any NPE, privacy, or living-relative considerations.

Scenario B: The Yeoman's Family

You are researching the Sutton family of a Cheshire manor between 1580 and 1700. You have post-1538 parish register evidence and want to extend the line into the manorial record period. You have found: a baptism for Thomas Sutton in 1618 at the parish church; a marriage for Thomas Sutton and Alice Browne in 1644; a burial for Thomas Sutton in 1691; a manorial court roll of 1689 recording Thomas Sutton's surrender of a copyhold messuage to his son James; an inquisition post mortem of 1608 recording the death of one Thomas Sutton of this manor, with a son also named Thomas described as aged 5; and a subsidy roll of 1598 listing a William Sutton as taxable in this township.

Research task: Using these sources, construct a research dissertation establishing what the Sutton family line looks like between 1580 and 1700, how each piece of evidence contributes to the case, what gaps remain, and what further records would extend or confirm the line. Include ethical reflection on any considerations of historical sensitivity or public accessibility of findings.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Write a full professional research dissertation for either Scenario A or Scenario B above. Your dissertation should meet all six components: research context and question; methodology; evidence analysis; proof argument (GPS-compliant); ethical reflection; and professional contribution and future directions. Aim for 1,200–1,800 words. Every factual assertion must be cited. Demonstrate the full range of professional genealogical competency expected at Lead tier.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Model Dissertation: Scenario B — The Sutton Family of Cheshire, 1580–1700

1. Research Context and Question

This dissertation investigates the Sutton family of [Manor Name], Cheshire, with the aim of constructing a documented family line for the period 1580–1700 and establishing continuity between the documented post-1538 parish record period and the earlier manorial record period. The research question is: Can a continuous, evidence-based Sutton family line be established for this Cheshire manor from the subsidy roll entry of 1598 through to the documented manorial succession of 1689?

2. Methodology

The research strategy proceeded from the most recent and most directly documented evidence (the 1689 court roll) backwards, supplementing documentary records with manorial records for the pre-parish period. Sources selected for priority investigation: parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) at the relevant church; the 1689 manorial court roll (original at Cheshire Archives, ref. [reference]); the 1608 inquisition post mortem (TNA, WARD 7/[ref]); the 1598 lay subsidy roll for the relevant hundred (E 179/[ref]). The logical sequence moved from known to unknown: establishing Thomas Sutton (b. 1618) first, then tracing backwards through the IPM to identify his father, and considering whether William Sutton in the 1598 subsidy roll may be the grandfather of Thomas (b. 1618).

3. Evidence Analysis

The 1689 court roll (original source; primary information) directly records Thomas Sutton's surrender of a copyhold messuage to his son James. This establishes: that Thomas held copyhold land; that he had a son James; and that the transaction occurred in 1689. His 1691 burial (parish register, original source, primary information) places his death two years after the surrender — consistent with a dying man disposing of his copyhold before death.

Thomas's 1618 baptism entry is original, primary evidence. His 1644 marriage to Alice Browne provides a second original, primary record. These form the documentary core of his biography.

The 1608 IPM (original source, primary information for land held; secondary for stated age of heir) records the death of a Thomas Sutton of this manor with a son Thomas aged five. This provides indirect evidence that a second Thomas Sutton (b. c.1603) existed — older than the baptised Thomas of 1618 by approximately 15 years. This discrepancy requires resolution (see below).

The 1598 subsidy roll lists William Sutton as taxable in this township. This is primary evidence for William's presence; indirect evidence that he was a householder of some means. No direct connection between William and Thomas (b. 1618) or the 1608 IPM's Thomas is established by any single source.

Conflict resolution: The 1608 IPM describes a Thomas Sutton with a son aged 5 (b. c.1603). The baptism register records a Thomas Sutton baptised in 1618. These cannot be the same person. Resolution: the IPM's Thomas is either a different individual of the same name (a father-son naming pattern is common in this period and confirmed by the IPM itself), or the 1618 baptism represents a later child of the same name after the 1603 child died. The second explanation is supported by the absence of any burial for a Thomas Sutton in the parish register between 1603 and 1618. The first explanation is supported by the manorial court roll's Thomas Sutton (still living and active in 1689 at apparent age c.71 if born 1618) — plausible but at the outer range of likely age for an active landholder. Further research (see section 6) is needed to resolve this.

4. Proof Argument

Research question: Was there a continuous male Sutton line in this Cheshire manor from William Sutton (subsidy roll, 1598) to James Sutton (manorial court roll admission, 1689)?

Survey: Records consulted include subsidy rolls, parish registers, manorial court rolls, and the 1608 IPM. The parish registers were searched for all Sutton entries 1580–1700; no other William Sutton appears in this period. No burial for a Thomas Sutton (the IPM child) appears in the register pre-1618.

Analysis: The preponderance of the available evidence supports a three-generation Sutton male line: William Sutton (present 1598, taxable householder) → Thomas Sutton the elder (died before/by 1608; subject of IPM, son aged 5) → Thomas Sutton the younger (baptised 1618; married 1644; surrendered copyhold 1689; buried 1691) → James Sutton (admitted to copyhold 1689). However, the 1608 IPM's Thomas Sutton had a son aged 5 (b. c.1603) — 15 years older than the baptised Thomas of 1618. This gap is not explained by current evidence. The hypothesis that the 1618 Thomas is a second son of the 1608 Thomas (the first son dying young without a burial record or surviving) is plausible but remains unproven.

Conclusion: The available evidence supports with moderate confidence a continuous Sutton male line in this manor across the period, with the specific relationship between the 1608 IPM and the 1618 baptism identified as an unresolved conflict requiring further investigation before the line can be stated with reasonable certainty.

5. Ethical Reflection

This research involves no living individuals. The historical records are in the public domain and held at accessible archives. One ethical consideration arises from the use of manorial records: the 1689 court roll records a specific property transaction; any living descendants of James Sutton may have historical family tradition about this property, and a researcher publishing this work should be aware that historical property claims can occasionally generate current family interest. The published findings should be stated factually and carefully — not in a way that implies current legal claims.

6. Professional Contribution and Future Directions

This research extends the documented Sutton line back to the 1608 IPM and tentatively to the 1598 subsidy roll — a century of manorial continuity. To extend further and to resolve the 1603/1618 discrepancy, the following records should be consulted: the full series of manorial court rolls (to identify any Thomas Sutton admission between 1603 and 1644); the Cheshire probate registry for a will of Thomas Sutton dying before 1608 (which may name children); and any further subsidy rolls or lay tax assessments for the period 1570–1600 that may name William Sutton's parents. The research is suitable for publication in the Cheshire Genealogist or submission as a case study in a society journal, subject to resolution of the identified conflict.
learningObjectives: Produce a six-component professional research dissertation demonstrating GPS-standard evidence analysis, proof argument writing, and professional reflection.
Integrate documentary and DNA evidence within a single coherent research argument.
Demonstrate ethical reasoning about any sensitive dimensions of the research project.
Articulate the professional contribution of the research and the direction of future investigation.
commonMistakes: Writing a narrative without a structured proof argument — the dissertation requires a formal GPS-compliant argument, not just a family history story.
Omitting the ethical reflection section — this is required and demonstrates the lead-level professional awareness that distinguishes this tier from SENIOR.
Failing to acknowledge unresolved conflicts or limitations — intellectual honesty is itself a professional quality being assessed.
Writing the methodology as a research log ('first I searched, then I found...') rather than as a strategic account ('the parish registers were selected because...').
assessmentCriteria: Research methodology (25%): sources are strategically selected with explicit justification; search strategy is logical and comprehensive; negative evidence is documented.
Evidence analysis (25%): GPS source/information/evidence framework applied throughout; conflicts identified and addressed with principled resolution.
Proof argument (25%): all five GPS elements present; conclusion language appropriately qualified; limitations acknowledged.
Professional reflection (25%): ethical considerations addressed substantively; professional contribution articulated; future research directions identified.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The application material for the Certified Genealogist credential; includes a proof argument and other portfolio items demonstrating GPS-standard research, citing, analysis, and professional conduct.
The style guide and submission requirements for the National Genealogical Society Quarterly — the benchmark for genealogical academic publication quality.

The complete Genealogical Proof Standard: (1) reasonably exhaustive search; (2) complete, accurate citations; (3) analysis and correlation of evidence; (4) resolution of conflicting evidence; (5) soundly reasoned, coherently written conclusion.

A proof argument addresses a single genealogical question; a dissertation encompasses a broader research project including context, methodology, multiple evidential analyses, ethical reflection, and professional contribution.

questions.questionHtml: What distinguishes a professional research dissertation from a proof argument?
options: A dissertation is longer but otherwise identical in structure

A dissertation encompasses a broader project including research context, methodology, multiple evidence analyses, proof argument, ethical reflection, and professional contribution — not just a single GPS-compliant argument
A dissertation does not need to meet GPS standards
A proof argument is for US researchers; a dissertation is for UK researchers
questions.correctAnswer: A dissertation encompasses a broader project including research context, methodology, multiple evidence analyses, proof argument, ethical reflection, and professional contribution — not just a single GPS-compliant argument
questions.explanationHtml: A proof argument addresses a single genealogical question through the GPS framework. A professional research dissertation is a broader document that situates the research in context, explains the strategic methodology, applies evidence analysis across multiple sources, includes a formal proof argument, reflects on ethical considerations, and articulates the work's professional contribution and future directions.

questions.questionHtml: In your dissertation methodology section, you describe the research as: 'First I searched Ancestry, then I searched FindMyPast, then I searched FamilySearch.' What is wrong with this methodology section?
options: Platform-based search descriptions are acceptable in a methodology section

This is a chronological research log, not a strategic methodology — the methodology section should explain which record types were selected, why they were expected to address the research question, and what the logic of the search sequence was
You should not mention specific platforms by name in a professional dissertation
The methodology section should list only the records that yielded positive results
questions.correctAnswer: This is a chronological research log, not a strategic methodology — the methodology section should explain which record types were selected, why they were expected to address the research question, and what the logic of the search sequence was
questions.explanationHtml: A professional methodology section explains the reasoning behind the research strategy: why specific record types were selected (not platforms), what each was expected to contribute to the specific research question, and what the logical sequence of investigation was. A chronological log tells the reader what was done; a methodology tells them why, which is more informative and demonstrates professional judgment.

questions.questionHtml: Your dissertation research reveals an unresolvable conflict between two sources — both reliable, both original, both giving different information about a key relationship. How should you handle this in the proof argument section?
options: Choose the source that supports your preferred conclusion and omit the other
Average the two sources' information for a compromise position

State the conflict explicitly, explain why it cannot currently be resolved with available evidence, indicate what further research would resolve it, and reflect this residual uncertainty in the conclusion's qualified language
Publish only the sources that agree and note that conflicting sources exist in a separate private research file
questions.correctAnswer: State the conflict explicitly, explain why it cannot currently be resolved with available evidence, indicate what further research would resolve it, and reflect this residual uncertainty in the conclusion's qualified language
questions.explanationHtml: GPS requires resolution of conflicts — and the honest acknowledgement that some conflicts cannot be resolved with currently available evidence. A dissertation that acknowledges an unresolvable conflict and identifies future research directions demonstrates higher professional maturity than one that suppresses a conflict. The conclusion's language should accurately reflect this residual uncertainty.
